title: Blockchain Security Audit Checklist

source.name: Cyfrin Solodit — Blockchain Security Audit Checklist

export_note: Partial export of the interactive checklist page (captured 2026-08-03). The live checklist tracks 370 items; this capture contains the 25 items whose Description/Remediation/References were visible. Reference numbers (#1, #2, ...) are placeholders preserved verbatim from the source page. Section headers that were visible without captured items are listed as empty sections — no content is fabricated for them.

items.title: Is the withdrawal pattern followed to prevent denial of service?
items.description: To prevent denial of service attacks during withdrawals, it's critical to follow the withdrawal pattern best practices - pull based approach.
items.remediation: Implement withdrawal pattern best practices to ensure that contract behavior remains predictable and robust against denial of service attacks.

items.title: Is there a minimum transaction amount enforced?
items.description: Enforcing a minimum transaction amount can prevent attackers from clogging the network with zero amount or dust transactions.
items.remediation: Disallow transactions below a certain threshold to maintain efficiency and prevent denial of service through dust spamming.

items.title: How does the protocol handle tokens with blacklisting functionality?
items.description: Tokens with blacklisting capabilities, such as USDC, can pose unique risks and challenges to protocols.
items.remediation: Account for the possibility of blacklisting within token protocols to ensure continued functionality even if certain addresses are blacklisted.

items.title: Can forcing the protocol to process a queue lead to DOS?
items.description: Forcing protocols to process queues, like a queue of dust withdrawals, can be exploited to cause a denial of service.
items.remediation: Design queue processing in a manner that is resilient to spam and cannot be exploited to cause denial of service.

items.title: What happens with low decimal tokens that might cause DOS?
items.description: Tokens with low decimals can present issues where the transaction process fails due to rounding to zero amounts.
items.remediation: Implement logic to handle low decimal tokens in a way that prevents the transaction process from breaking due to insufficient token amounts.

items.title: Does the protocol handle external contract interactions safely?
items.description: Protocols must handle interactions with external contracts in a way that does not compromise their functionality if external dependencies fail.
items.remediation: Ensure robust handling of external contract interactions to maintain protocol integrity regardless of external contract performance.

items.title: Does the protocol rely on `balance` or `balanceOf` instead of internal accounting?
items.description: Attackers can manipulate the accounting by donating tokens.
items.remediation: Implement internal accounting instead of relying on `balanceOf` natively.

items.title: Are "get-or-create" patterns protected against front-running attacks?
items.description: Functions combining resource creation and interaction (like getOrCreateAndUse) are vulnerable to front-running attacks where attackers can create the resource with different parameters before the victim, potentially manipulating prices or conditions.
items.remediation: Separate creation and interaction into distinct transactions or implement robust protections (parameter validation, relative references instead of absolute values) to ensure safe operation regardless of creation timing.

items.title: Are two-transaction actions designed to be safe from frontrunning?
items.description: Actions that require two separate transactions may be at risk of frontrunning, where an attacker can intervene between the two calls.
items.remediation: Ensure critical actions that are split across multiple transactions cannot be interfered with by attackers. This can involve checks or locks between the transactions.

items.title: Can users maliciously cause others' transactions to revert by preempting with dust?
items.description: Attackers may cause legitimate transactions to fail by front-running with transactions of negligible amounts.
items.remediation: Implement checks to prevent transactions with non-material amounts from affecting the contract's state or execution flow.

items.title: Is the protocol using a properly user-bound commit-reveal scheme?
items.description: Sensitive on-chain actions can be exposed in the mempool, enabling frontrunning and information exploitation. Effective commit-reveal schemes must bind commitments to specific users and transactions.
items.remediation: Implement a two-phase process where users first commit a hash containing their address and all transaction parameters, then reveal actual actions after the commitment phase ends, preventing frontrunning and information leakage.

items.title: Is there an external function that relies on states that can be changed by others?
items.description: Malicious actors can prevent regular user transactions by making a slight change to the on-chain states.
items.remediation: Ensure normal user actions especially important actions like withdrawal and repayment are not disturbed by other actors.

items.title: Can the contract operations be manipulated with precise gas limit specifications?
items.description: Attackers can supply carefully calculated gas amounts to force specific execution paths in the contract, manipulating its behavior in unexpected ways.
items.remediation: Implement explicit gas checks before critical operations.

items.title: Is block.timestamp used for time-sensitive operations?
items.description: Miners can manipulate block.timestamp by several seconds, potentially affecting time-dependent contract logic.
items.remediation: Use block.number instead of timestamps for critical timing operations or ensure manipulation tolerance is acceptable.

items.title: Is the contract using block properties like timestamp or difficulty for randomness generation?
items.description: Block properties (timestamp, difficulty) and other predictable values should not be used for randomness as they can be influenced or predicted by miners.
items.remediation: Use a secure randomness source like Chainlink VRF, commit-reveal schemes, or a provably fair randomization mechanism instead.

items.title: Is contract logic sensitive to transaction ordering?
items.description: Miners control transaction ordering and can exploit this for front-running, back-running, or sandwich attacks.
items.remediation: Implement protection by allowing users to specify acceptable results that revert transactions when breached.

items.title: Is the price calculated by the ratio of token balances?
items.description: Price can be manipulated via flash loans or donations if it is derived from the ratio of token balances.
items.remediation: Use the Chainlink oracles for the asset prices.

items.title: Is the price calculated from DEX liquidity pool spot prices?
items.description: Spot price readings derived directly from DEX liquidity pools are vulnerable to manipulation through flash loans that can temporarily drain the pools.
items.remediation: Use TWAP (time-weighted average price) with appropriate time windows based on asset volatility and liquidity, or use reliable oracle solutions.

items.title: Is there any state change after interaction with an external contract?
items.description: Untrusted external contract calls could callback leading to unexpected results such as multiple withdrawals or out-of-order events.
items.remediation: Use check-effects-interactions pattern or reentrancy guards.

items.title: Is there a view function that can return a stale value during interactions?
items.description: Read-only reentrancy occurs when a view function, called during a reentrant execution, returns inaccurate data because the contract's state is temporarily inconsistent due to an ongoing external call, potentially misleading dependent protocols.
items.remediation: Apply the Check-Effects-Interactions pattern to prevent inconsistent state, and ensure the reentrancy guard state is not ENTERED for critical view functions to prevent returning stale data.

items.title: Are there protections against replay attacks for failed transactions?
items.description: Failed transactions can be susceptible to replay attacks if not properly protected.
items.remediation: Implement nonce-based or other mechanisms to ensure that each transaction can only be executed once, preventing replay attacks, even if the transaction initially failed.

items.title: Is there protection against replaying signatures on different chains?
items.description: Signatures that are valid on one blockchain may be replayed on another, leading to potential security breaches.
items.remediation: Use chain-specific parameters, such as `block.chainid`, or domain separators as defined in EIP-712 to ensure signatures are only valid on the intended chain.

items.title: Can the admin of the protocol pull assets from the protocol?
items.description: Some protocols grant an admin with a privilege of pulling assets directly from the protocol. In general, if there is an actor that can affect the user funds directly it must be reported.
items.remediation: Allow access to only the relevant parts of protocol funds, e.g. by tracking fees internally. Forcing a timelock on the admin actions can be another mitigation.

items.title: Does the protocol have an explicit slippage protection on user interactions?
items.description: An attacker can monitor the mempool and puts two transactions before and after the user's transaction. For example, when an attacker spots a large trade, executes their own trade first to manipulate the price, and then profits by closing their position after the user's trade is executed.
items.remediation: Allow users to specify the minimum output amount and revert the transaction if it is not satisfied.

items.title: Is there a mechanism depending on the number of users?
items.description: It is very easy to trigger actions using a lot of alternative addresses on blockchain. Any quorum mechanism or utilization based rewarding system can be vulnerable to sybil attacks.
items.remediation: Do not rely on the number of users in quorum design.
